nameStory: The Eastern Panthea gets its name from its geographic range in eastern North America, distinguishing it from its western cousins. The genus name 'Panthea' comes from Greek mythology, referring to a goddess associated with all divine powers - perhaps a nod to this moth's impressive presence and striking appearance.
description: The Eastern Panthea is a medium-sized moth with distinctive fuzzy, tufted caterpillars that feed on evergreen trees like pines and spruces. Adults have a wingspan of about 1.3 to 2 inches and display attractive mottled patterns in grays and browns. These moths belong to the large cutworm moth family, though their caterpillars don't cut plants at ground level like their notorious relatives. You're most likely to spot the adults attracted to lights during summer evenings.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Forewings show intricate mottled patterns of gray, brown, and white that create excellent camouflage against tree bark when the moth rests with wings folded roof-like over its body

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wingspan typically 1.3-2 inches across, noticeably larger than many common house moths but smaller than giant silk moths

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: Thick, fuzzy body covered in dense scales that feel soft to the touch, with a robust thorax typical of strong-flying night moths

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: When at rest during the day, holds wings in a steep tent-like position over the body, pressed close to tree bark where the mottled pattern provides excellent camouflage

idTips.label: Antenna Shape
idTips.description: Males have feathery, thread-like antennae that feel delicate and branched, while females have simpler, thinner antennae

habitat: Look for Eastern Panthea moths in coniferous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially areas with healthy populations of white pine, red spruce, and eastern larch (tamarack). They're found from sea level to mid-elevations in the mountains, wherever their host trees grow. The moths are often attracted to lights near cabins, campsites, or homes adjacent to evergreen forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not active yet in spring. Look for overwintering pupae in soil or leaf litter beneath pine and spruce trees.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight time from June through August when adults emerge and are attracted to lights at night. This is the best time to spot them, especially on warm, humid evenings.
seasonality.fall: In southern New England, a second generation may emerge in early fall. Caterpillars are actively feeding on evergreen needles and can be found on pine and spruce branches.
seasonality.winter: Moths spend winter as pupae underground. No adults or caterpillars visible, though you might find old cocoons or pupal cases in the soil.

funFact: The caterpillars of Eastern Panthea moths are sometimes called 'tufted white pine caterpillars' because they sport dramatic tufts of hair that look like tiny punk rock mohawks, making them one of the most fashionably styled caterpillars in New England forests!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the closely related Black Zigzag Moth, but Eastern Panthea tends to have more mottled, less contrasted wing patterns. Memory trick: Eastern Panthea has 'blended' patterns like eastern forests mix different tree types, while Black Zigzag has sharper, more defined zigzag lines.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cutworm moth,' the Eastern Panthea's caterpillars don't actually cut plants at soil level like true cutworms. Instead, they feed up in the tree canopy on evergreen needles, showing how diverse this large moth family can be in their feeding habits.
compareHints: The Eastern Panthea differs from its close relative the Black Zigzag Moth by having more subdued, mottled wing patterns rather than sharp black zigzag markings. Eastern Panthea also tends to be slightly larger and has a more northerly distribution in New England. Both species share similar fuzzy caterpillars that feed on conifers, but the Black Zigzag caterpillars typically have more pronounced tufts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Black Zigzag Moth can be distinguished from its close relative, the Eastern Panthea Moth, by its more pronounced and sharply defined zigzag markings - the Eastern Panthea has more subtle, wavy lines and tends to be slightly larger overall.
